info.name: Software Cryptography Provider
info.description:
# Software Cryptography Provider

Manual test collection for the Cryptography Provider **v2** REST surface. The v1 surface is unchanged and served alongside it; nothing here touches it.

## Running the connector locally

The connector needs PostgreSQL. Start one and point the connector at it:

```sh
docker run --rm -d --name softcp-db -p 5432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=softcp -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=softcp -e POSTGRES_DB=softcp postgres:18

JDBC_URL='jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/softcp' JDBC_USERNAME=softcp JDBC_PASSWORD=softcp \
  mvn -B spring-boot:run
```

## Using this collection

Import the collection and the environment beside it, then run the folders in order. The first folder needs nothing but the connector. The second creates a token the first time it addresses one, creates a key, and uses it: run it top to bottom, since the requests pass the key handles between them through collection variables.

`tokenName`, `keyAlias` and `keyCreationId` are per-run values. Change them, or re-import the environment, before running the second folder again.

## What the v2 surface does differently

- A request carries its token as attributes; there is no operation that creates, activates or removes one, so a token comes into existence the first time a context names it.
- A key is addressed by the metadata the connector published for it, one handle per half of a key pair.
- Everything completes inline. Asynchronous execution is refused and no operation is ever tracked.
- Failures are RFC 9457 problem documents carrying an `errorCode`, which is what the tests here assert.

The import requests carry a throwaway RSA-2048 key as their material, generated for this collection and protected under a passphrase kept beside it in the environment. Neither guards anything: they exist so an import can be exercised without the platform. Replace both to import a key of your own.

request.description: Reports the connector and the interfaces it serves. The cryptography interface is at v2 and declares key import. Asynchronous execution and key export are deliberately not offered. Needs no database.

exec: pm.test("cryptography is served at v2", function () { var i = pm.response.json().interfaces.find(function (x) { return x.code === "cryptography"; }); pm.expect(i.version).to.eql("v2"); });

pm.test("asynchronous execution is not declared", function () { var i = pm.response.json().interfaces.find(function (x) { return x.code === "cryptography"; }); pm.expect(i.features || []).to.not.include("asynchronous"); });

request.description: The whole attribute registry, with the connector version that defined it. Includes what the operations need to be told, which earlier interfaces never published.

exec: pm.test("signature attributes are published", function () { var names = pm.response.json().definitions.map(function (d) { return d.name; }); pm.expect(names).to.include("data_sigDigest"); });

request.description: One definition by its connector-global identifier.

exec: pm.test("it is the key alias attribute", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().name).to.eql("data_keyAlias"); });

request.description: One definition by its connector-global identifier.

exec: pm.test("the token selection attribute is defined", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().name).to.eql("data_existingToken"); });

request.description: A definition this connector does not publish is a problem document naming RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND.
The schema a token is configured with. This is what the token context in the next folder is built from.
Liveness of the connector itself.

exec: pm.test("liveness and readiness are reported", function () { var c = pm.response.json().components; pm.expect(c).to.have.property("liveness"); pm.expect(c).to.have.property("readiness"); });
pm.test("the correlation id comes back", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("correlation-id")).to.be.a("string"); });

request.description: Liveness of the connector itself.
Liveness of the connector itself.
Status reports rather than fails. A token the context names but that has never been used is reported Disconnected: it is created the first time an operation addresses it.
The usages a key of this provider can serve. It signs, verifies, encrypts and decrypts; it does not wrap keys.

exec: pm.test("usages are sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.eql(["sign", "verify", "encrypt", "decrypt"]); });

request.description: Only key pairs are offered. Secret keys are not implemented, so the provider does not offer to hold one.
What a key is created from: the alias, the algorithm, and the group whose contents follow the algorithm chosen. Creates the token if the context names one that does not exist yet.

Creates an RSA key pair synchronously. Each half comes back with its own durable handle in keyMeta, which the operations below send back to address that half. Repeating this request with the same keyCreationId returns the same key rather than making a second one.

exec: pm.test("a key pair was created", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().keyRequestType).to.eql("keyPair"); });
pm.test("the public key travels as SPKI", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().publicKeyData.keyData.publicKeySpki).to.be.a("string"); });
pm.test("no tracking handle for finished work", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().operationMeta).to.be.oneOf([undefined, null]); });
var reference = function (half) { return body[half].keyMeta.find(function (m) { return m.name === "meta_keyReference"; }).content[0].data; };

request.description: The same request again. A caller that lost the first response must be given the key it made, not a second key.

exec: pm.test("the same private key comes back", function () { var body = pm.response.json(); var reference = body.privateKeyData.keyMeta.find(function (m) { return m.name === "meta_keyReference"; }).content[0].data; pm.expect(reference).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("privateKeyReference")); });

request.description: Asynchronous execution is not offered. The connector refuses it rather than accepting work it finishes immediately, which would leave the caller polling for an operation that no longer exists.
What signing with this key needs to be told, which follows the key's algorithm: an RSA key needs a scheme and a digest.

exec: pm.test("the RSA scheme and digest are asked for", function () { var names = pm.response.json().map(function (a) { return a.name; }); pm.expect(names).to.eql(["data_rsaSigScheme", "data_sigDigest"]); });

request.description: Signs one item with the private key half. The signature comes back correlated by the identifier the request gave it.

exec: pm.test("one signature, correlated", function () { var s = pm.response.json().signatures; pm.expect(s).to.have.lengthOf(1); pm.expect(s[0].identifier).to.eql("one"); });

request.description: Verifies that signature with the public key half. Verification is always synchronous.
Encrypts with the public key half. Only RSA keys can be used this way, which is why the cipher schema is empty for the other algorithms.

exec: pm.test("the item identifier came back", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().encryptedData[0].identifier).to.eql("one"); });

request.description: Decrypts it again with the private key half, which must return the original bytes.

exec: pm.test("the original message came back", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().decryptedData[0].data).to.eql("c2VjcmV0IG1lc3NhZ2U="); });
pm.test("the item identifier came back", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().decryptedData[0].identifier).to.eql("one"); });

request.description: Random data from the provider, which needs a token context but no key.
Nothing is ever accepted for asynchronous processing, so nothing is ever tracked.
Key import is offered and declared. Key export is not, which is also why an import asking for a key that stays exportable is refused.

exec: pm.test("key pairs can be imported", function () { var t = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(t[0].keyRequestType).to.eql("keyPair"); pm.expect(t[0].algorithms).to.include("RSA"); });

request.description: Key import is offered and declared. Key export is not, which is also why an import asking for a key that stays exportable is refused.

exec: pm.test("an import asks only where to keep the key", function () { var a = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(a.map(function (x) { return x.name; })).to.eql(["data_keyAlias"]); });

request.description: Key import is offered and declared. Key export is not, which is also why an import asking for a key that stays exportable is refused.

exec: // The material is a throwaway RSA-2048 key generated for this collection and protected under
// importPassphrase. It guards nothing: it exists only so the import can be exercised locally.
// Replace both environment values to import a key of your own.

pm.test("both halves come back", function () { var k = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(k.publicKeyData.keyData.publicKeySpki).to.be.a("string"); pm.expect(k.privateKeyData.keyMeta).to.be.an("array"); });
pm.test("the key was imported under the reference the platform supplied", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.eql(200); });

request.description: Key import is offered and declared. Key export is not, which is also why an import asking for a key that stays exportable is refused.

exec: pm.test("the same key comes back", function () { pm.expect(JSON.stringify(pm.response.json().privateKeyData.keyMeta)).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("importedKeyMeta")); });

request.description: Key import is offered and declared. Key export is not, which is also why an import asking for a key that stays exportable is refused.

exec: pm.test("it reports the key that was imported", function () { pm.expect(JSON.stringify(pm.response.json().result.privateKeyData.keyMeta)).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("importedKeyMeta")); });

request.description: Key export is offered and declared. Only a key created or imported as exportable may leave the token.

exec: pm.test("key pairs can be exported", function () { var t = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(t[0].keyRequestType).to.eql("keyPair"); pm.expect(t[0].algorithms).to.include("RSA"); });

request.description: Key export is offered and declared. Only a key created or imported as exportable may leave the token.

exec: pm.test("an export asks for nothing", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.eql([]); });

request.description: Key export is offered and declared. Only a key created or imported as exportable may leave the token.

exec: pm.test("the key comes back protected", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().material.encryptedPrivateKeyInfo).to.be.a("string"); });
pm.test("the identity the request stated is echoed", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().keyReference).to.eql(pm.environment.get("keyReference")); });
pm.test("a key pair is described by its public key", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().keyData.publicKeySpki).to.be.a("string"); });

item.name: POST keys/export (a key that may not leave, expect 422)

request.description: Key export is offered and declared. Only a key created or imported as exportable may leave the token.

exec: // The created key above stated keyExportable false, so it stays in the token.
pm.test("it says the key was never allowed out", function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().errorCode).to.eql("KEY_NOT_EXPORTABLE"); });

request.description: Destroys the key the metadata addresses. Run it twice: the second attempt is answered as absent.
The same key once more. A key destroyed once is gone, and the answer says so rather than failing obscurely.
